disease-biology|pig.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: swine thrombin partly tracked humans—thrombin peak 242.35 nM (~50% of human 484.25) and production 93.6 nM/min (~84% of human 111.51), but swine produced no detectable plasmin. n=20; absent plasmin limits pig utility for fibrinolysis/disease-biology comparisons.
key_numbers: Thrombin peak 242.35 nM (~50% of human 484.25, n=20)
Thrombin production rate 93.6 nM/min (~84% of human 111.51, n=20)
Plasmin peak: not detected (human 457.20 nM, n=20)
Plasmin production rate: not detected (human 34.80 nM, n=20)

disease-biology|horse.summary: Evidence is mixed: horse tenocyte gene expression best matches human under transient inflammation (Mahalanobis 9.59) but is farther under healthy (23.05) and constant inflammation (12.97). Proliferation difference is large in healthy (slope 0.3000, p<2e-16) but negligible in transient inflammation (slope 0.0233, p=0.49).
key_numbers: 9.59 — Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes, transient inflammation)
23.05 — Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes, healthy)
12.97 — Mahalanobis distance to human (all genes, constant inflammation)
0.3000 — proliferation slope difference to human (healthy; p<2e-16)
0.0233 — proliferation slope difference to human (transient inflammation; p=0.4868)
disease-biology|horse.why_range_is_wide: Similarity varies by inflammatory state (healthy vs transient vs constant inflammation).

disease-biology|non-human primate.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: baboon and rhesus thrombin measures closely matched human values (thrombin peak 434 nM and 399 nM vs human 484 nM; thrombin production 124 and 111 nM/min vs 111.5 nM/min). However plasmin production rates were substantially higher (baboon 90.8 vs human 34.8 nM/min).
key_numbers: Baboon thrombin peak 433.78 nM (human 484.25 nM)
Rhesus thrombin peak 398.95 nM (human 484.25 nM)
Baboon thrombin production 124.22 nM/min (human 111.51 nM/min)
Rhesus thrombin production 111.22 nM/min (human 111.51 nM/min)
Baboon plasmin production 90.81 nM/min (human 34.80 nM/min)
disease-biology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Different metrics diverge: thrombin parameters approximate human values while plasmin generation—especially production rate—is much higher in primates.

disease-biology|d. melanogaster.summary: Zong et al. 2023: genome-wide transcript concordance between D. melanogaster and C. elegans exceeded c=0.1 for most within-stage comparisons (modest cross-species similarity); one larval pair (ce.lar–dm.lar) had c=0.087. Links to human disease are indirect, so translation is limited.
key_numbers: most within-stage Drosophila–C. elegans genome-wide c-scores >0.1
ce.lar–dm.lar genome-wide c-score = 0.087

disease-biology|rabbit.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: rabbit thrombin peak 71.6 nM (~15% of human 484.25 nM) and thrombin production 14.9 nM/min (~13% of human 111.51), while plasmin peak 197.7 nM (~43% of human 457.20) and plasmin production 17.6 nM/min (~51% of human 34.80). Rabbit curves were highly variable, so alignment with human coagulation is mixed.
key_numbers: 71.6 nM thrombin peak (rabbit) = 15% of human 484.25 nM
14.9 nM/min thrombin production (rabbit) = 13% of human 111.51 nM/min
197.7 nM plasmin peak (rabbit) = 43% of human 457.20 nM
17.6 nM/min plasmin production (rabbit) = 51% of human 34.80 nM/min
disease-biology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Different coagulation metrics diverge: thrombin measures are much lower than human while plasmin measures are nearer human values, and rabbit curves showed high variability.

disease-biology|c. elegans.summary: Zong et al. 2023: C. elegans shows modest, inconsistent concordance with disease-related expression—most C. elegans–Drosophila within-stage genome-wide c-scores >0.1, but one pair (ce.lar–dm.lar) was 0.087. Findings vary by stage pairings.
key_numbers: >0.1: genome-wide c-score for most C. elegans–Drosophila within-stage comparisons (Zong et al. 2023)
0.087: genome-wide c-score for ce.lar–dm.lar (Zong et al. 2023)
disease-biology|c. elegans.why_range_is_wide: Varies by developmental stage pairings—most within-stage comparisons exceed 0.1 but specific pairs (e.g., ce.lar–dm.lar) are lower (0.087).

disease-biology|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: rats mirror human biology in some domains (26/30 blood variables changed same way post-exercise, Goutianos et al. 2015; behavioral/electrophysiological correlations, Der-Avakian et al. 2025) but not others (≈50% transcriptome DEG alignment, Vacca et al. 2024; lower thrombin/plasmin peaks vs human, Tarandovskiy et al. 2020). A CDAA-fed rat MASLD model had MHPS = 0.941 for MASH-fibrosis (Vacca et al. 2024).
key_numbers: 26/30 blood variables changed toward same direction after exercise (Goutianos et al. 2015)
1/19 biomarkers showed species×exercise interaction (Veskoukis et al. 2016)
≈50% whole-transcriptome DEG alignment with humans (Vacca et al. 2024)
MHPS = 0.941 for CDAA-fed rat MASH-fibrosis (Vacca et al. 2024)
Rat thrombin peak 270.28 nM vs human 484.25 nM (Tarandovskiy et al. 2020)

disease-biology|sheep.summary: Oreff et al. 2021 found sheep tenocytes matched human tenocytes mainly under constant inflammation (Mahalanobis 8.94) but diverged under healthy conditions (Mahalanobis 24.78); MMP genes were relatively close (8.6) while inflammatory mediators were farther (18.51). n=3 biological replicates/species; some slope differences were small but significant (proliferation diff −0.0878, p=0.009).
key_numbers: Mahalanobis 8.94 — all genes under constant inflammation
Mahalanobis 24.78 — all genes under healthy conditions
Mahalanobis 8.6 — MMPs (MMP1, MMP3, MMP13)
Mahalanobis 18.51 — inflammatory mediators (COX2, IL6)
Proliferation slope difference −0.0878 vs human under constant inflammation (p=0.009)
disease-biology|sheep.why_range_is_wide: Similarity shifts with inflammatory state (healthy vs transient vs constant) and varies by gene set.

efficacy|mouse.summary: Pan et al. 2020: mouse tumor-growth-inhibition (TGI) did not predict clinical approval—median TGI 0.74 for approved vs 0.77 for failed drugs and AUC=0.45 for predicting approval; odds ratios for higher TGI quartiles vs lowest were 0.74–0.90 and non-significant. Comparisons are limited by few approved drugs and variable TGI measurement across studies.
efficacy|mouse.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: Median TGI 0.74 (approved drugs)
Median TGI 0.77 (failed drugs)
AUC = 0.45 for TGI predicting approval
OR = 0.74–0.90 for Q2–Q4 vs Q1 (all <1)
P-trend = 0.636 (no association)
efficacy|mouse.why_range_is_wide: OR range reflects separate comparisons of TGI quartiles Q2–Q4 versus Q1.

disease-biology|mouse.summary: Evidence is mixed: some mouse–human transcriptome comparisons agree (Takao et al. 2015: Spearman r 0.43–0.68; 77–93% genes same direction), but others show near‑zero genome‑wide concordance (Seok et al. 2013: R^2 ≤0.09; Kodamullil et al. 2017: 12% genes mimicked).
key_numbers: R^2 ≤0.09 — genome-wide correlation human vs mouse gene-expression changes (Seok et al. 2013)
47–63% — genes changing in same direction human vs mouse (Seok et al. 2013)
0.43–0.68 — Spearman r for human vs mouse fold-changes (Takao et al. 2015)
77–93% — genes changing same direction human vs mouse (Takao et al. 2015)
12% — human-deregulated genes mimicked by mouse models (Kodamullil et al. 2017)
disease-biology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Ranges arise from different models, thresholds, timepoints and whether analyses use genome-wide vs pathway/leading‑edge gene sets.
disease-biology|mouse.negative_controls_noted: Seok et al. 2013 notes the 'same direction' metric has a ~50% random baseline.

efficacy|rodent.summary: Rodent efficacy findings did not reliably predict clinical efficacy: O'Collins et al. 2006 found similar mean neuroprotection in focal ischemia for drugs tested only in animals (24.4%) and drugs used clinically (31.3%, p>0.05), and translation rates ranged 0–100% (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022). Many preclinical studies (82%) reported positive findings, suggesting publication/selection bias.
efficacy|rodent.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: 24.4% mean improvement in focal models for drugs tested only in animals (n=351)
31.3% mean improvement in focal models for drugs also used clinically (n=66)
62% of focal ischemia results were superior to control (animal studies)
82% of preclinical animal studies reported positive findings
0–100% range of reported translation rates from animal to human studies
efficacy|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Translation rates came from heterogeneous studies and outcomes across reviews and were affected by publication bias and selective reporting.

efficacy|non-rodent.summary: Leenaars et al. 2019 provides no direct efficacy data; for toxicity it reports non‑rodent→human concordance for liver effects 40% (n=951) and that animal data predicted 48% of 221 human adverse drug reactions. They also report 71% concordance when all species are pooled and state predictivity is higher for non‑rodents than rodents.
key_numbers: 40% — concordance of liver effects (non‑rodent→human; n=951)
48% — proportion of human adverse drug reactions predicted from animal data (221 events)
71% — concordance when all species considered
efficacy|non-rodent.why_range_is_wide: The 71% figure pools all species; 40% is the non‑rodent-specific concordance for liver effects.

safety-pharmacology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence shows NHP cardiovascular safety findings largely track human results: Bhatt et al. 2019 — combined BP+HR sensitivity 78%, specificity 79% (NPV 92%), though HR-only sensitivity was 54%. Sadko et al. 2024 found NHP moxifloxacin QTc +10.9 ms (vs ~10 ms in humans).
key_numbers: 78% sensitivity — large animal to human (combined BP+HR)
79% specificity — large animal to human (combined BP+HR)
92% negative predictive value — combined BP+HR
54% sensitivity — large animal to human (HR only)
10.9 ms QTc increase — NHP moxifloxacin (matches ~10 ms in humans)
safety-pharmacology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by endpoint: combined BP+HR concordance is higher than HR-only.
safety-pharmacology|non-human primate.negative_controls_noted: Sadko et al. 2024 included a mock (no-effect) drug showing no QTc change up to 3× clinical concentration.

safety-pharmacology|rat.summary: Bhatt et al. 2019: Rat findings tracked large-animal changes for combined BP+HR (sensitivity 84%, specificity 71%, PPV 90%, NPV 60%) but were weaker for single endpoints (HR sensitivity 64%, BP specificity 59%) and 23–26% showed opposite direction of change. Predictive values may be inflated because dataset prevalence may be lower than real-world.
key_numbers: 84% — sensitivity for combined BP+HR (rat→large animal)
71% — specificity for combined BP+HR (rat→large animal)
90% — positive predictive value for combined BP+HR (rat→large animal)
64% — sensitivity for HR only (rat→large animal)
23–26% — opposite direction of change for HR/BP (rat→large animal)
safety-pharmacology|rat.why_range_is_wide: The 23–26% range reflects separate opposite-direction percentages reported for HR versus BP.

safety-pharmacology|dog.summary: Dogs moderately predict human cardiac safety: Valentin et al. 2022 found 91% of drugs that prolonged QT in humans also prolonged QT in dogs (88% concordant negatives; 31% discordant), and Pollard et al. 2017 reported dog QTc AUC ≈0.81. Bhatt et al. 2019 gave combined BP/HR sensitivity 78% and specificity 79%, and Sadko et al. 2024 observed moxifloxacin +16.6 ms QTc in dogs (human ≈10 ms); concordance varies by endpoint and exposure.
key_numbers: 91% of human QT‑prolonging drugs also prolonged QT in dogs (Valentin et al. 2022)
88% of drugs with no human QT effect also showed no effect in dogs (Valentin et al. 2022)
Dog QTc AUC ≈0.81 versus clinical QTc (Pollard et al. 2017)
Sensitivity 78% / Specificity 79% for large‑animal→human combined BP/HR (Bhatt et al. 2019)
Moxifloxacin +16.6 ms QTc in dogs vs ~10 ms in humans (Sadko et al. 2024)
safety-pharmacology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Variation arises by endpoint (QTc vs BP/HR), assay type and exposure level, and dataset composition (e.g. inclusion/exclusion of β2‑agonists).
safety-pharmacology|dog.negative_controls_noted: Sadko et al. 2024: mock/vehicle produced no QTc increase (negative control).

toxicology|dog.summary: Evidence is mixed — dog data sometimes track human toxicities for specific endpoints (dog LR+ for cardiac disorders 6.11; regulatory rat+dog testing flagged 71% of human toxicities (Jang et al. 2019)). However absence of dog toxicity gives only modest reassurance (~72% no human toxicity; dog iNLR≈1.10).
key_numbers: 72% — probability of no human toxicity given no dog toxicity (Bailey et al. 2019)
Dog median iNLR = 1.10 (Bailey et al. 2015)
LR+ = 6.11 for dog, cardiac disorders (Clark et al. 2018)
Specificity 84% and NPV 86% for predicting absence of clinical adverse effects (beagle dog; Monticello et al. 2017)
71% — human toxicities correctly predicted by regulatory testing in rats and dogs (Jang et al. 2019)
toxicology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by organ class, endpoint and toxicity severity (e.g., cardiac vs hepatic, grade 3–4 vs all grades, in vitro vs in vivo).

toxicology|rabbit.summary: Evidence is mixed: rabbit tests show signal for some cardiac endpoints (Clark et al. 2018: rabbit LR+ 3.54 for cardiac disorders; QT prolongation post-test odds 83%). But overall animal-to-human discriminative weight is minimal (Bailey et al. 2015: rabbit median iNLR 1.12).
key_numbers: LR+ 3.54 — rabbit, cardiac disorders (Clark et al. 2018)
QT post-test odds 83% — rabbit, QT prolongation (Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ 2.8 — rabbit, hepatobiliary disorders (Clark et al. 2018)
median iNLR 1.12 — rabbit-human (Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by endpoint and dataset selection (overall selectivity low while specific cardiac endpoints show higher concordance).

toxicology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: NHP findings sometimes predict human toxicity — Monticello 2017 overall sensitivity 48% and specificity 84% (GI PPV 91%, nervous PPV 83%), and Clark 2018 LR+ up to 11.02. But other analyses report weak or inconsistent prediction (Bailey 2019 no-animal→no-human 70.4%; Bailey 2015 iNLR 1.02).
key_numbers: Sensitivity 48% (Monticello et al. 2017)
Specificity 84% (Monticello et al. 2017)
GI PPV 91% / Nervous PPV 83% (Monticello et al. 2017)
LR+ 11.02 (cynomolgus, hepatobiliary; Clark et al. 2018)
No-animal-toxicity → no-human-toxicity 70.4% (Bailey et al. 2019)
toxicology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by organ/endpoint, toxicity severity, study selection bias and low clinical positive prevalence.

toxicology|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: some studies find rat findings often align with human toxicity (regulatory tests predicted 71% of human toxicities; rat LR+ 4.73 for cardiac and 2.74 for hepatobiliary), but other analyses show only modest predictive power (median PPV 0.65; iNLR 1.82). Variation by endpoint, severity and study methods limits generalisability.
key_numbers: 71% — regulatory tests (rats+dogs) correctly predicted human toxicities
LR+ 4.73 — rat, cardiac disorders
LR+ 2.74 — rat, hepatobiliary disorders
median PPV 0.65 — rat, all toxicity grades
median iNLR 1.82 — rat
toxicology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Results vary by endpoint, toxicity grade and study methods/datasets (e.g., Jang pooled rats and dogs; Atkins stratified by severity).

toxicology|mouse.summary: Mouse toxicology is mixed: some mouse signals predict human toxicity (Clark et al. 2018 — LR+ cardiac 5.29; hepatobiliary 3.73; pain 7.4). However overall discrimination is weak (Atkins et al. 2020 median PPV 0.57 all grades, 0.43 for grade 3–4; Bailey et al. 2015 iNLR 1.39).
key_numbers: LR+ cardiac (mouse–human) = 5.29 (Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ hepatobiliary (mouse–human) = 3.73 (Clark et al. 2018)
LR+ pain (mouse–human) = 7.4 (Clark et al. 2018)
Median PPV all toxicity grades (mouse) = 0.57 (Atkins et al. 2020)
Mouse iNLR = 1.39 (Bailey et al. 2015)
toxicology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Results vary by specific organ endpoint and toxicity severity (Clark shows high LR+ for some endpoints; Atkins shows PPV falls for grade 3–4).

toxicology|rodent.summary: Monticello et al. 2017: rodent toxicology showed modest sensitivity (48%) and PPV (43%) but higher specificity (84%) and NPV (86%), so rodent findings only partially tracked human adverse effects. Performance varied by organ (PPV 0–54%; e.g. Ophthalmology 0%, Biochemical 54%) and was poor for subjective 'other' events (PPV 9%, NPV 14%).
key_numbers: Sensitivity 48% (overall, detecting clinical adverse effects)
PPV 43% (overall)
Specificity 84% (overall)
NPV 86% (overall)
PPV range 0–54% across organs (Ophthalmology 0%, Biochemical 54%)
toxicology|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Predictive values differ by target organ and event type; subjective 'other' events had especially low PPV/NPV.

efficacy|sheep.summary: Perel et al. 2007: in ewe models antenatal corticosteroids were linked to higher neonatal mortality (pooled OR 12.5, 95% CI 1.9–79.2), which contrasts with no benefit in clinical trials — sheep results did not track human outcomes. The estimate is imprecise.
efficacy|sheep.direction: evidence does not favour the model
key_numbers: 12.5 (95% CI 1.9–79.2) — pooled OR for neonatal mortality in ewe models (antenatal corticosteroids)
efficacy|sheep.why_range_is_wide: Very wide CI reflects few and/or small ewe experiments giving imprecise estimates.

toxicology|zebrafish.summary: Zebrafish assays generally track human toxicology: McGrath et al. 2008 detected 100% of teratogens and 75% of non‑teratogens; Cornet et al. 2017 reported 78% accuracy (89% specificity, 68% sensitivity). Performance varies by endpoint (neuro 54% vs hepatotoxicity 80%).
key_numbers: 100% teratogens detected (McGrath et al. 2008)
75% non‑teratogens identified (McGrath et al. 2008)
78% overall accuracy (Cornet et al. 2017)
89% specificity and 68% sensitivity overall (Cornet et al. 2017)
toxicology|zebrafish.why_range_is_wide: Sensitivity differs by toxicity endpoint (e.g. neurotoxicity 54% vs hepatotoxicity 80%).

veterinary|dog.summary: Dog models recapitulated many human cancer transcriptomes, with robustness scores up to 85.05% (adult bladder) and several tumors ≥70% (pediatric glioma 79.88%, adult head & neck 78.20%). However, suitability varied by tumor type and negative controls (ACC, LAML) scored low (adult ACC 31.10%).
key_numbers: 85.05% — model robustness score for adult bladder cancer
79.88% — model robustness score for pediatric glioma
78.20% — model robustness score for adult head and neck cancer
72.95% — model robustness score for pediatric sarcoma
31.10% — model robustness score for adult adrenocortical carcinoma (negative control)
veterinary|dog.why_range_is_wide: Scores vary across cancer types (adult vs pediatric and tumor lineage) and include deliberate negative-control cancers.
veterinary|dog.negative_controls_noted: Negative controls reported: adult adrenocortical carcinoma 31.10%, pediatric adrenocortical carcinoma 33.56%, adult leukemia (LAML) 40.31%.
